title: Pooled Buyer Mandates for Group Discounts
one_liner: Thousands of buyer agents sign standing purchase mandates ('I will pay up to $X if 200 others join') and vendors bid to fill the pooled demand.
customer: Startups and SMBs (10-200 employees) buying SaaS and business services (renewals, business insurance, telecom). Buyers pay a success fee and vendors pay for pre-committed demand.
problem: Small buyers lack bargaining power and time, and group purchasing organizations serve hospitals and enterprises, not the long tail. Vendors offer volume discounts against committed volume they cannot see. Agent payment standards now include signed intent mandates (Google's AP2, Mastercard's Verifiable Intent) that capture limits and constraints, and AP2 explicitly anticipates group scenarios, yet no product pools them.
solution: A mandate pool where each buyer or their agent signs an intent mandate with price ceiling, term and threshold. The exchange aggregates by category, shows vendors a live demand curve with reservation prices, and runs a sealed-bid reverse auction when the threshold is met. Purchases execute through each buyer's own payment mandate. First category: annual SaaS renewals, a Vendr for the long tail.
why_now: AP2 (September 2025), Verifiable Intent and UCP provide the first standard way to hold cryptographically signed, pre-authorized purchase intent. Agents now run procurement tasks, and vendors moving to agent meters want volume signals.
revenue_model: 5-10% of buyer savings or a 2-4% vendor fee on pooled transactions.
non_obvious_insight: A signed intent is a binding, machine-readable limit order for goods, so small buyers can pre-commit credibly without a human negotiating. That credibility is what makes group buying scale, like Kickstarter for procurement.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 startups from a founder community to pledge to 5 popular tools through a web form (protocol integration later). Bring the demand curve to 5 vendors and close one pooled deal to prove price.

title: Burn Boss: Prescribed Fire as a Service
one_liner: AI burn-window planning, permits, drone ignition crews and liability cover, so landowners can safely burn and insurers can pay for the risk reduction.
customer: Private landowners, ranchers, timber owners, prescribed burn associations, water districts and utilities in TX, OK, OR, CA and CO. Insurers and reinsurers later pay for outcomes.
problem: Prescribed fire is the most effective fuel-reduction tool and the least scaled. Barriers are burn-plan expertise, weather windows, permits and smoke filings, liability insurance and crew logistics, not the fire itself.
solution: Start with a burn-plan generator and weather-window alerts built on AI forecast ensembles, plus a permit and smoke-filing packet, sold to burn associations. Then add a drone-ignition operator network and a liability wrap through a partner MGA. Add verified before/after fuel maps that insurers can underwrite (check state burn-liability rules).
why_now: AI weather models became operational in 2025 (such as ECMWF's AIFS), drone aerial ignition has matured, and record reinsurance capital wants provable mitigation. Several states have been reforming burn liability law (verify).
revenue_model: $1-3K per burn plan, per-acre service fees, and later outcome payments from carriers or utilities.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is planning and liability, not fire. Insurers can pay because treated acreage lowers their probable maximum loss.
first_30_days: Join 3 burn associations, ship window alerts and the plan generator, and run 5 paid burns.

title: Clickwrap Gatekeeper: Agents Buy Contract Counsel
one_liner: An API agents call before clicking 'I agree'. It returns clause-level risk against the principal's delegated-authority policy, plus a signed archive of exactly what was accepted.
customer: Wallet-holding consumer and enterprise agents, and the platforms that run them, paying $0.02-$0.50 per document evaluation plus an evidence-archive fee per acceptance. Agent-wallet and browser-agent vendors are the natural embedders.
problem: Agents will accept tens of thousands of ToS, DPAs, auto-renewals, arbitration waivers and data-resale clauses for people and companies. Courts increasingly treat automated assent as binding, so the open legal question is the scope of the agent's authority. Agents can read a contract, but none has a legal-grade policy engine or a defensible evidence trail. Amazon's fight with Perplexity over agent access is one visible example of that unsettled authority.
solution: check(url_or_text, policy) diffs the document, hash-cached and versioned, against the principal's policy: max liability, no auto-renew beyond 30 days, no mandatory arbitration, no resale of personal data. It returns ALLOW, ESCALATE or REFUSE with cited clauses. On ALLOW it snapshots the page (hash, timestamp, screenshot) into a tamper-evident log so the principal can later prove what was accepted. A diff feed alerts the principal when terms change on services already accepted. It is positioned as a policy engine, not legal advice, with law-firm-authored policy packs.
why_now: Agent authority is the live legal question of 2026, with law-firm memos on 'authority to bind' and litigation over agent access. Payment protocols such as AP2 mandates and ACP mean agents now click through payment terms without a human present. Browser agents are in production use.
revenue_model: Metered evaluation (first-seen documents priced high, cache hits nearly free), an evidence-archive fee per accepted contract, enterprise policy packs, and a marketplace for lawyer-written policy templates with a revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of legal risk in the agent economy is not the model's hallucination but the tiny irrevocable assent. Because most ToS are near-identical templates, one shared cache amortizes legal analysis across millions of agents, which no single company can do for itself. Lawyers become policy authors rather than reviewers, and gross margin exceeds 90% once the cache is warm.
first_30_days: Crawl and index ToS, privacy and DPA pages for the top 5,000 SaaS and e-commerce sites and cluster them into templates. Publish a free MCP server with 1,000 free checks. Recruit 3 advisory lawyers to seed policy templates. Pitch agent-wallet startups and browser-agent vendors to embed it as a pre-payment check, and start charging in month 2.

title: CPAP Off-Ramp: Retire Machines, Refurbish for Uninsured
one_liner: Re-test sleep apnea at each weight-loss milestone, help patients who have gone into remission safely come off CPAP, and refurbish the retired machines for the newly uninsured.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans and self-insured employers (paying a share of avoided rental and supply costs), cash-pay GLP-1 patients paying for the recheck, and safety-net clinics buying refurbished units.
problem: Tirzepatide is approved for moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity, and in SURMOUNT-OSA 43% to 52% of patients at the top dose met disease-resolution criteria, with apnea-hypopnea events cut by up to about 60%. Nobody is paid to notice. DME suppliers earn on continued mask and hose resupply, sleep labs earn on tests, and patients keep machines in the closet. After 13 months of Medicare rental the patient owns the machine, so it can simply be donated. Meanwhile about 4.8M people are newly uninsured after the ACA subsidy expiry, with millions more Medicaid losses due in 2027, and a $800-1,000 CPAP is out of reach.
solution: A physician-supervised pathway with a disposable home sleep apnea test at each 10% weight-loss milestone and a telehealth sleep-physician review. Patients who qualify taper or stop PAP, and are offered a buy-back credit or donation. Returned machines are sanitized, function-tested, data-wiped and re-kitted with new humidifier chambers, filters and tubing, then re-issued via licensed DME partners and clinics at roughly $150-250. Motors, foam and plastics from units that fail go to recycling.
why_now: Zepbound's OSA indication is now established and Part D can cover it. The cash-pay pill wave and the July 2026 Medicare Bridge bring far more patients on-drug. ACA and Medicaid losses create a cash-pay buyer base for cheap devices.
revenue_model: Performance fee from payers or employers of about 30% of first-year avoided rental and supply cost. Cash-pay recheck ($79-129). Margin on refurbished device sales, with a nonprofit partner able to receive donation tax deductions.
non_obvious_insight: GLP-1 success silently strands both a recurring billing stream and a physical asset. The party that finds the stranded machine can be paid twice: once by the payer for the avoided spend and once by the uninsured buyer for the second life.
first_30_days: Contract a tele-sleep physician group and a licensed DME partner. Recruit 100 patients from a cash-pay telehealth partner who have OSA and are on tirzepatide. Write the refurbishment SOP against manufacturer cleaning guidance and state DME rules. Sell the first payer or employer pilot on a savings-share basis with retrospective claims data.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for Downstream Payers
one_liner: Recover itemized tariff surcharges from suppliers who were refunded the tariffs, on contingency, and give surcharge-collecting firms a defensive ledger.
customer: Small contractors, restaurants, repair shops and retailers who were invoiced a separate 'tariff surcharge' line by suppliers in 2025-26, plus small firms that added such surcharges to their own customers' bills.
problem: SCOTUS ruled on 2026-02-20 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, and about $166B in CBP refunds go to the importer of record (about $81B paid by July). Over 40% of small firms saw tariff cost increases and 76% of international sourcers passed them on, so the firm that paid the pass-through gets nothing. Each claim is too small ($200-$8k) for a lawyer, and firms that billed surcharges to their own customers now carry their own exposure.
solution: Read-only scan of the owner's mailbox and QuickBooks/Xero pulls every tariff or surcharge line from vendor invoices and from the firm's own customer invoices. It builds a two-sided surcharge ledger (paid upstream, collected downstream), then generates supplier demand letters that cite the invoice wording and contract terms. Unpaid claims escalate to small-claims templates or a partner attorney. Claims are strongest where the invoice said the surcharge was itemized or refundable. Because one supplier can owe hundreds of customers, settlements can be negotiated per supplier instead of per claim.
why_now: Refunds have been flowing through CBP's automated system since April 2026, so suppliers are holding refund cash right now, before it is absorbed into margins. Invoice records are fresh and 2026 books have not closed.
revenue_model: 25-30% contingency on recovered dollars, with a $49 flat fee for the ledger and audit. Later, a per-supplier settlement-program fee.
non_obvious_insight: Refund law is written for importers, but the money trail is an invoice trail. Itemized invoices are contract evidence, and thousands of tiny claims against a few hundred suppliers form a portfolio no law firm will touch. The same ledger doubles as a defense file for firms that billed surcharges.
first_30_days: Offer a free 'surcharge audit' in trade-specific Facebook groups and subreddits (HVAC, restaurant equipment, apparel resellers). Hand-review 50 mailboxes and find the 10 suppliers with the most itemized surcharges. Retain a consumer-protection attorney to review the demand-letter template, send the first 100 letters, and measure the response rate.

title: Robotaxi Revenue-at-Risk Ratings for Airports and Cities
one_liner: A quarterly exposure index and analyst service that estimates how much airport parking, meter and citation revenue, and the bonds backed by it, will erode as robotaxis scale city by city.
customer: Municipal bond investors and credit research desks, rating and bond insurance analysts, airport and city CFOs and parking operators, and regional lenders holding parking-heavy real estate collateral.
problem: Parking and ground transportation account for roughly 43-45% of airports' non-aeronautical revenue in North America. Waymo now serves Phoenix, San Jose, SFO (curbside) and San Antonio, where a round-trip robotaxi fare of $15-25 undercuts the $30-150 an airport earns on a multi-day parking stay. Cities depend on meters and citations, and garage cash flows collateralize loans. Nobody underwrites this transition; disclosures are scattered across PDFs.
solution: Structure the data from airport financial reports, bond official statements and city ACFRs, then combine it with AV service-area maps, expansion announcements, ride-hail share and ground-transport fee schedules. Publish per-airport and per-city 'percentage of revenue at risk' under three adoption scenarios, plus fee-design advice (AV-specific trip fees, dynamic parking). Ship a free public index to build authority, then sell subscriptions, alerts and consulting.
why_now: Waymo reports 500k paid weekly rides, launched Denver, San Diego and Tampa on September 1 (14 commercial cities), and targets 1M weekly rides by year-end. LAX is already raising per-trip TNC fees to $6. Airports and cities are scrambling for a playbook and investors have no model.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $12-40k per year for buy-side and rating shops, $25-100k consulting engagements with airports and cities, and custom risk screens for lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The first place AVs bite public finance is not jobs, it is the parking-fee cash flows pledged to bonds that everyone treats as stable. The data is public but unstructured, so a two-person team with careful extraction can build a moat before larger research houses look.
first_30_days: Extract parking and ground-transport revenue lines for the top 30 US airports and 20 cities from public reports. Build a simple three-scenario model and publish a free index and a short note. Send it to 50 muni credit analysts and airport finance officers and sell the first five paid subscriptions.

title: Year-Three Warranty Claims Agent and Failure Index
one_liner: An agent that files manufacturer, retailer and credit-card extended-warranty claims when your stuff dies, paid on success, whose claims data becomes a durability index that Amazon's star ratings cannot provide.
customer: Consumers who bought $200 to $3,000 durables (appliances, e-bikes, laptops, mattresses, power tools) in the past 1 to 4 years. Later data buyers: home-warranty and insurance firms, retailers, brand quality teams and AI shopping agents.
problem: Amazon's incentives end at the return window, and reviews freeze at week two, but failures happen in year two to four. The money left behind sits in three layers: manufacturer warranties, retailer protection plans and credit-card extended warranty. It goes unclaimed because people cannot find the receipt, do not know which layer applies, or quit at the phone tree. Meanwhile shoppers have no independent durability signal, and the one consumer tool for spotting fake reviews, Fakespot, was shut down by Mozilla in July 2025 for lack of a business model.
solution: The consumer connects a receipt source (read-only, receipts only, opt-in) and the agent builds a coverage ledger for big purchases: warranty end dates, card-benefit eligibility, retailer plan status. When the user texts that the dishwasher died, the agent assembles the claim packet (receipt, serial number, photos, symptom), files with the right layer over email, chat or a voice agent, and chases it to resolution. Every outcome (brand, model, failure mode, age at failure) goes into an anonymized Failure Index.
why_now: LLM agents can now read messy receipts and run multi-channel claims at a cost per claim low enough for a success-fee model. AI shopping assistants and agentic checkout need trustworthy durability signals, which star ratings do not supply. Fakespot's 2025 shutdown proved consumers will not pay to check reviews, so the payer has to be the claim recovery itself.
revenue_model: A success fee of 20% to 25% of recovered value (refund, repair or replacement), or $19 flat per filed claim. In year two, license the Failure Index by API or report to warranty administrators, insurers, retailers and shopping agents ($2k to $25k per month). Affiliate referrals for a better replacement at the moment of failure.
non_obvious_insight: The unowned moment in commerce is month 25, not the purchase. Every incumbent (Amazon, brands, card issuers) profits when claiming is hard, and a failure someone bothered to claim is a labeled ground-truth data point, unlike a star rating. Sell claims recovery to consumers, who will pay, and the byproduct dataset is what the institutions that price durability will pay for.
first_30_days: Run it concierge-style. Put up a landing page: 'Did your appliance, e-bike or laptop die within 3 years? We file the claim, you pay only if we recover.' Recruit 30 claimants from Reddit (r/appliances, r/ebikes) and local Facebook groups. Draft claims with an LLM and send them by hand, logging every outcome. Pick one category (for example e-bike batteries or robot vacuums) and publish five public posts on what the claims data shows. Approach one home-warranty or appliance-retail company for a paid data pilot.

title: Heat-Health Desk for Medicare Advantage Plans
one_liner: Forecast-triggered outreach and cooling delivery for the heat-vulnerable members whose hospital bills the health plan pays.
customer: Medicare Advantage, D-SNP and Medicaid managed-care plans in the Southwest, Southeast and Pacific Northwest (supplemental-benefits and medical-director teams).
problem: Summer 2026 brought the hottest US July on record and a European heatwave with about 38,000 provisional deaths (secondary source). Heat waves drive ER visits and admissions among older, medicated, low-income members. Plans pay the downstream cost but do not know which members lack working cooling or live on top floors. Cooling supplemental benefits are underused.
solution: Risk-stratify members by housing type, utility arrears, medications that impair heat tolerance and prior heat visits. Trigger phone outreach ahead of forecast heat, deliver and install AC or fans through partners, run check-in calls on days 1-3, and help prevent utility shutoffs. Report avoided ER visits.
why_now: After the 2026 heat shock, plan medical directors are looking for concrete heat programs. Off-season (Oct-Feb) is when supplemental-benefit budgets get set.
revenue_model: Per targeted member per month in season, or per intervention, plus shared savings.
non_obvious_insight: The party that absorbs the cost of heat is the health plan, not the city. Heat is a claims-management problem and belongs in the plan's budget.
first_30_days: Use public hospital heat-visit data to build a cost-per-heat-day case. Pitch 5 regional plans for a 2,000-member pilot next season, and line up an AC-delivery and check-in vendor.

title: Whey Capture Skids for Small Cheesemakers
one_liner: Leased containerized filtration skids that turn small cheese plants' cheap whey into sellable protein concentrate.
customer: Regional and farmstead cheese plants that sell whey for pennies or pay to dispose of it.
problem: Whey protein is scarce and pricey, yet small plants lack the ultrafiltration equipment and offtake to capture it, because equipment makers sell to giants.
solution: A leased, containerized ultrafiltration and diafiltration skid on revenue share, producing liquid whey protein concentrate that we sell to partner dryers and beverage makers.
why_now: Whey concentrate is up 108% in two years and isolate reaches $14/lb, so the byproduct now outearns its economics at small scale.
revenue_model: Skid lease plus a 30-40% revenue share on concentrate sold.
non_obvious_insight: The byproduct ate the product, and the largest untapped upside sits with small plants that big equipment vendors ignore.
first_30_days: Tour five plants in WI, VT and CA, quote a used UF skid, and pre-sell offtake to one beverage brand and one dryer.

title: Reusable Trust Passport for Bio-AI Access
one_liner: One neutral, portable verification that a biotech or academic lab is legitimate, bound to that lab's agent keys, so frontier AI vendors and DNA/reagent suppliers can accept its agent-placed orders without repeating the diligence.
customer: Small and mid-size biotechs, academic labs and CROs that need relaxed AI safeguards and want agents to order DNA, oligos and reagents. Secondary payers are AI vendors and suppliers who pay per verified check.
problem: On September 17, 2026 Anthropic launched its Life Sciences Verification Program (credential, security and ethics-oversight review, 30-day data retention) and expected hundreds of organizations in week one. Other AI providers, DNA synthesis vendors and cloud labs will each build their own version. Small labs lack SOC 2-style security paperwork, organized IBC documentation or an ethics-oversight file, so they queue or get denied. Machine identities already outnumber humans about 109 to 1 and there is no shared 'know your agent' standard for bio orders.
solution: A one-time dossier (organization identity, IBC/IACUC registration, named biosafety officer, lightweight security review, data-handling policy) issued as a verifiable credential tied to the lab's agent keys. AI vendors and suppliers accept it for access tiers and agent-placed orders, and the credential is continuously monitored and revoked if an IBC approval lapses. Include a readiness checklist and concierge help to complete the paperwork.
why_now: Verification programs started in September 2026, creating an immediate backlog and duplicative-paperwork problem. Agent-order volume is growing, and synthesis-screening rules and frontier-lab safeguards are tightening at the same time.
revenue_model: Flat verification fee ($1.5-5K one-time plus annual renewal), per-check fees from vendors and AI providers, and an enterprise tier for CRO networks and shared core facilities.
non_obvious_insight: Frontier labs cannot be each other's trust anchor, which is why an accredited third-party reviewer that several of them accept is valuable. This is the Vanta/Plaid pattern applied to bio access, and the first concierge revenue comes from the backlog, before any network effect exists.
first_30_days: Build the 'verification readiness' checklist and offer a $2.5K flat concierge service to the first 20 labs that applied. Talk to 3 mid-tier DNA/oligo vendors and 2 cloud labs about accepting your dossier for agent orders. Publish an open template so vendors see you as the standards-setter, then charge for review and monitoring.

title: Launch-or-Rebook Guarantees for Rocket-Chasing Travelers
one_liner: A 'Launch Flex' add-on that hotels, charters and viewing events sell to fans, promising a rebook credit or refund if the target launch slips or scrubs, priced from launch history and weather.
customer: Space Coast and Starbase-area lodging, boat and viewing charters, ticketed viewing events and tour companies. Fans buy the add-on, and operators keep most of the premium.
problem: With 321 orbital launches in 2025 and Starship reaching orbit on 28 Sep 2026, launch-chasing has become a travel subculture. Dates slip and scrub, rates are non-refundable, and fans hesitate to commit. Operators either eat cancellations or lose bookings, and launch-night price spikes breed disputes.
solution: An embeddable add-on for operators' booking pages ($19-49). If the target launch slips beyond a defined window, the guest gets a rebook credit for the next launch or a partial refund. Risk is priced by vehicle, pad, provider and season from public launch logs and weather, starting as an operator-issued credit and later reinsured by a parametric MGA partner.
why_now: New vehicles and pads (Stoke's $1B raise, Starship orbital operations) add schedule variance and fans. Lead times are shrinking (37.5 to 33 days), and firm launch dates appear only days out. The launch-tourism audience is growing faster than operators' booking tools.
revenue_model: The platform keeps about 30% of the add-on premium, operators pay a $99 monthly widget fee, and later parametric-underwriting margin is added.
non_obvious_insight: A launch is a public, well-logged binary event with years of slip history, which makes travel risk easier to price than weather. Rebook credits let a hotel convert a demand spike into repeat visits instead of refunds.
first_30_days: Build a slip and scrub model from public launch logs. Sign 5 Titusville and Cocoa Beach hotels and 2 charter operators to pilot the add-on on their booking pages, and start collecting fees on the next 10 launches.

title: Thermosphere Density Nowcasts From Mega-Constellation Orbits
one_liner: A live atmospheric-drag API that uses the drag on thousands of satellites as a planetary sensor grid.
customer: Mid-size LEO operators, space situational awareness vendors (as an OEM component), launch providers, insurers, and reentry-risk teams.
problem: Drag uncertainty is the dominant error in LEO conjunction assessment and reentry prediction. With over 10,000 Starlinks in orbit and Solar Cycle 25 storms hitting low shells, operators face false-alarm maneuvers, wasted propellant and surprise reentries. Existing density models are coarse.
solution: Assimilate public element sets and published satellite ephemerides to infer density by altitude, latitude and time. Deliver a nowcast plus a 72-hour forecast as an API and as a plug-in for flight-dynamics tools. Sell reduced false-alarm rates and better reentry windows, with validation reports.
why_now: The mega-constellation means the sensors are already in orbit and free. The briefing reports about 10,413 Starlinks. Storm risk persists near the solar maximum. New operators are moving to lower shells and need better drag forecasts.
revenue_model: $50-250k per year per operator. OEM licensing to SSA vendors. Event-based storm reports for insurers and launch providers.
non_obvious_insight: For space traffic, the sensor is not scarce, the model is. The largest calibration dataset ever assembled is flying overhead for free.
first_30_days: Build a backtest against public geomagnetic-storm episodes using open element sets, and publish accuracy versus a standard model. Offer free access to three mid-size operators and one SSA vendor in exchange for feedback and a paid pilot.

title: Tariff Surcharge Credit-Memo Recovery for Mid-Size Manufacturers
one_liner: Mine a plant's accounts-payable history for 2025-26 tariff surcharges, then win credit memos from the distributors who are now receiving IEEPA refunds.
customer: US manufacturers with $5M-$200M revenue and 30-300 active vendors who paid line-item 'tariff surcharges' or tariff-justified price increases from March 2025 through the February 2026 Supreme Court ruling. The buyer is the CFO, controller or purchasing director.
problem: Refunds go to the importer of record, and importers of record are usually distributors: fastener houses, bearing and fitting suppliers, steel service centers, electronics distributors, tooling vendors. The plant paid the surcharge but has no claim with CBP. Downstream buyers have to rely on contract and unjust-enrichment theories against the vendor. Large retailers have law firms doing this, but a $4k-$60k claim per vendor is below any law firm's floor. Plant managers also will not sue the only source of a hydraulic fitting, so the claims are simply going unasked.
solution: 'SurchargeScan': connect to QuickBooks, NetSuite, Epicor or Infor (or upload AP PDFs). AI extracts surcharge lines and tariff-justified price-increase letters, ranks vendors by likelihood of being the importer of record (using public bill-of-lading data and vendor type), and generates reservation-of-rights letters. It then runs a relationship-preserving negotiation for credit memos against future orders instead of cash demands, and tracks each vendor's refund status through CBP's CAPE process. A partner law firm signs off on letters and escalates only large or hostile cases.
why_now: The Supreme Court held the IEEPA tariffs unlawful in February 2026. CBP launched its CAPE refund module on April 20, 2026, with well over $100B accepted for processing. The government is appealing the Court of International Trade's refund order, so vendors are receiving cash now while uncertainty still gives buyers leverage. Every month vendors book the windfall as profit, the claim gets harder to recover.
revenue_model: 20%-25% contingency on recovered credits and cash, plus a $499 scan fee credited against the fee. Average expected recovery of $25k-$150k per plant, with margins on a heavily automated flow. Later, an ongoing 'duty-pass-through audit' for any future tariff regime.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody in the surcharge fight wants to be in court with their own supplier. Plant managers will happily take a credit memo on the next PO but will never file a lawsuit, so the winning product is a diplomatic credit negotiation run by software, not a demand-letter factory.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 Ohio plant controllers as design partners with a free scan in return for 20% on recoveries. Build the scanner with an LLM over exported AP data plus a public bill-of-lading lookup. Send 20 reservation-of-rights letters and get the first credit memos booked. Sign a referral and review agreement with one trade-law boutique. Publish the recovery rate data from the first 10 vendors to sell the next 50 plants.

title: Fill-Level Sensors for Remote Vault Toilets
one_liner: Satellite-capable fill-level and usage sensors for the vault toilets on public land and in campgrounds, so pump trucks go where and when they are actually needed.
customer: Campground and recreation concessionaires operating on federal and state land, state park systems, county park departments, ski areas and trailhead managers. Second wave: event, construction and portable-restroom fleets. Pumping contractors are channel partners.
problem: Vault toilets are pumped on fixed calendars or when a hiker reports an overflow. Busy sites need pumping weekly or monthly in peak season and remote sites once every year or two. Trucks drive one to three hours each way. A full toilet closes a site, damages the visitor experience, and holiday weekends generate emergency call-outs at premium rates.
solution: An ultrasonic or time-of-flight sensor puck under the riser lid plus a PIR visit counter, on LTE-M with a narrowband satellite (NB-NTN) fallback for no-coverage sites. The dashboard forecasts 'days to full' from usage and holiday and weather calendars, then auto-generates work orders to the nearest contractor with route batching. Usage counts also drive restocking of toilet paper and cleaning visits.
why_now: Narrowband satellite IoT modules and plans have reached commercial availability, cutting the cost of monitoring a toilet 40 miles from cell coverage. Recreation agencies and concessionaires face tight staffing and budgets, so triaging truck rolls has real value.
revenue_model: USD 12-20 per toilet per month including a leased sensor (about USD 150 hardware cost). A 600-toilet concessionaire is about USD 100k per year. Route-optimization module for pumpers. Event-fleet pricing per unit per event.
non_obvious_insight: The savings isn't fewer pump-outs; it's knowing which toilets are near-full before a holiday weekend and avoiding closures and emergency call-outs. Pumpers earn per visit, so pitch them a route-density and demand-forecast tool that grows their business rather than threatening it.
first_30_days: Build 30 units from off-the-shelf modules. Pilot 5-10 toilets each with three concessionaires and two county park departments. Use the shoulder season (hunting and early winter trailheads) to test. Recruit one septic pumping company as a co-pilot partner. Convert to annual contracts before next spring's opening.

title: Heatwave Demand Signals for Cool-Climate Hotels
one_liner: A revenue-management add-on that turns heatwave forecasts in origin cities into rate floors, minimum stays and direct-booking campaigns for hotels in cool refuge regions, days before the booking surge arrives.
customer: Independent hotels and guesthouses (20-150 rooms) and regional tourism boards in cool refuge regions: Scottish Highlands, Norwegian fjords, Galicia/Asturias/Cantabria, Baltic coast, Slovenian Alps, Irish west coast; in the US, the Oregon/Washington coast, Maine and Michigan's Upper Peninsula.
problem: Demand for cool regions surges within days of heat events in origin markets (London, Paris, Madrid, Milan, Chicago), but revenue managers set rates weekly from pace reports and holiday calendars. Booking lead times are shrinking (about 33 days versus 37.5). OTAs capture the last-minute surge at their own price, while 51% of European hotels already suspect OTAs of selling below loaded rates. Hotels underprice, sell out cheaply and lose direct-booking margin.
solution: Ingest open ensemble forecasts for roughly 150 origin metros. Calibrate lag and elasticity per hotel from its own booking curve (read-only PMS/channel-manager connection). Send a daily WhatsApp or email alert such as 'Heat dome over Madrid Thu-Sun; expect searches for Asturias to jump from Wednesday; raise floor 15%, add a 2-night minimum, push the direct offer to your Madrid and Barcelona email list.' Optionally trigger geo-targeted direct-booking ads and pre-approved regional DMO 'Cool Escape' co-op campaigns.
why_now: Summer 2026 produced rerouted, last-minute, value-driven travel (Europe ADR +4-6%, shorter lead times). Google AI Overviews now show hotel prices and reportedly cut metasearch click-through 31% in tests, so hotels must capture surges through their own channels. Booking's merchant model is eroding rate control. 'Coolcation' travel is mainstream enough that destinations market it openly.
revenue_model: $79-199 per month per property, an optional performance fee of 3% of incremental direct revenue, and DMO campaign licenses of $15-40K per season.
non_obvious_insight: Heat in the origin market is a public leading indicator that hotel systems are blind to, because they were built around event and holiday calendars. The edge is a 72-hour timing arbitrage against OTAs. It doubles as a dispersal tool, steering demand from saturated Mediterranean hotspots to under-visited regions that tourism boards are eager to promote.
first_30_days: Backtest July-August 2026 with 5 hotels' booking curves under NDA and quantify money left on the table during the heat dome. Publish the case study. Ship v0 as a Google Sheet plus a weather API plus WhatsApp alerts. Sell two regional DMO pilots (Galicia, Scottish Highlands) for a triggered spring campaign.

title: Funeral Home Land-and-Business Split Advisory
one_liner: An advisor that separates aging independent funeral directors' real estate from their operating business. The land goes to housing developers, the shrunken business is leased back or sold to a consolidator, and the advisor earns fees and a small equity slice.
customer: Owners of independent funeral homes (about 75% of 15,401 US funeral homes are family or privately owned), especially those over 60 without a successor. Infill housing developers and investors buy the land. Consolidators such as SCI and Everstory may buy the business.
problem: These sites were built for burial-era visitation: large buildings with big parking lots on prime corridors. With cremation at about 63%, flat deaths and volume down 1.4% at SCI, the buildings are oversized while taxes and upkeep rise. Owners get lowball offers for the business that bundle the land. Developers never see these parcels, which are off-market and not listed. The business buyer pool and the land buyer pool are disjoint and do not talk to each other.
solution: Screen parcels using zoning, lot size, transit and local cremation share, plus state licensing data on owner age. Offer owners a split: sell or ground-lease the land to a developer and lease back a compact 2,500-3,000 sf service footprint (or a ground-floor space in the new mixed-use building), or sell the business alone to a consolidator. Package parcels for states with single-staircase and missing-middle reforms. Sell paid feasibility studies first, then take closing fees and equity.
why_now: Single-staircase reform (7 states in 2025, Michigan in July 2026) and California AB 2074 lower infill costs. Rates near 7.5% make greenfield harder, so infill parcels gain appeal. Consolidator cash flow is strong (SCI operating cash flow up 43%), which makes them acquisitive. Cremation growth is making the buildings redundant.
revenue_model: $5-10K paid feasibility studies, a 2-3% success fee on the land transaction, 5-10% carried equity in the project, and a fee when the business is sold to a consolidator.
non_obvious_insight: Funeral homes are a large class of buildings whose function shrank while owners still think of them as businesses, not real estate. The highest and best use is often housing, and the key is to split the land from the operation so neither buyer pool discounts the other.
first_30_days: Pull funeral home parcels in two or three states with recent zoning reform. Contact 100 owners aged 60 or over (from state funeral-board license data). Sign three paid feasibility studies. Partner with one infill developer and one consolidator to test appetite.

title: Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers
one_liner: Independent pharmacies hold the half of the PBM ledger that employers never see, which is what the PBM actually paid the pharmacy. Pool it to run spread audits for self-insured employers, and give pharmacies a stay-or-leave calculator for their take-it-or-leave-it PBM contracts.
customer: Two sides. First, independent pharmacies, at $99-199 a month for benchmarking and a network-contract modeler. Second, self-funded local employers, school districts, counties and union funds (from 100 to 5,000 lives), plus the benefit consultants and TPAs that serve them, who pay per audit or a share of verified savings.
problem: The employer sees only what it paid the PBM. The PBM sees both sides and hides one. The pharmacy sees what it was paid and what it paid the wholesaler, but has no benchmark and no idea whether the network offer that arrives every Q4 for January 1 is worse than its peers' terms. Everyone negotiates blind. PBMs threaten a pharmacy with losing about a quarter of its business if it declines, and a plan sponsor cannot verify 'pass-through' claims.
solution: Read-only ingestion of the pharmacy's 835 remittance files and invoice costs from its pharmacy management system (PMS). Output 1) per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement benchmarked against NADAC and an anonymized peer pool. 2) A stay-or-leave model of each 2027 network offer built from the pharmacy's own claims mix. 3) With sponsor consent, a claim-level tie-out of the pharmacy-paid amounts against the employer's PBM claims file. That yields a true spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member, delivered as an audit the employer can use to renegotiate or move to a transparent PBM.
why_now: The contract season for January 2027 is happening right now, which gives a hard deadline and a free entry wedge. Employer fiduciaries are under pressure from ERISA suits over PBM costs, state PBM transparency laws and FTC scrutiny. Pharmacy closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores) have given local officials political will. OCR and LLM parsing of messy remit PDFs now makes onboarding a one-day job rather than a consulting project.
revenue_model: Pharmacy subscription of $99-199 a month, or free in exchange for data. Employer audit fees of about $8k-25k per mid-size sponsor, or 10-20% of first-year verified savings. Data licenses to state employee plans, attorneys general, employer coalitions and consultants at a higher tier.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone in the PBM fight holds half a ledger, and only the pharmacy can prove the gap. Thirty pharmacies in one county reconstruct the local school district's and county government's spread at claim level. Independents will hand this data over willingly because it is the first ammunition they have ever had against take-it-or-leave-it contracts.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 pharmacies through the state independent pharmacy association with the pitch 'we will model your 2027 PBM offers free'. Build parsers for the three biggest PBMs' remit formats (the 835 EDI standard helps). Deliver the first stay-or-leave reports. Hire a healthcare attorney to structure data-use terms, since provider-manual confidentiality clauses and HIPAA de-identification are the main risk. Offer one local school district or county a free pilot spread audit and turn the result into a one-page case study.

title: SOX Evidence Packs for Agent-Run Controls
one_liner: Control libraries, walkthrough scripts and test evidence that let auditors accept AI agents inside financial close, AP and reconciliations.
customer: Controllers, SOX program managers and internal audit at US public companies ($500M-$10B revenue) piloting agents in finance, plus mid-tier audit firms that must test them.
problem: As of mid-2026 the PCAOB has no AI-specific standard. Auditors ask how agent actions are authorized, logged and reviewed, and whether agent-generated walkthroughs count as sufficient evidence. FEI's Committee on Corporate Reporting published an AI-in-ICFR framework in June 2026, but finance teams have no packaged controls or evidence format.
solution: A library of agent-specific controls mapped to COSO 2013 (access, prompt and model change management, completeness, override monitoring), with test scripts, sampling templates and an evidence collector that exports action logs, approval trails and change tickets in auditor-ready format. Start with a pre-interim readiness assessment.
why_now: Calendar-2026 audits are entering interim testing, the June 2026 FEI framework gives a hook, and a standards vacuum means the first accepted evidence format wins.
revenue_model: $20-$60k readiness assessments, $3-$8k/month evidence subscriptions, and license deals with audit firms.
non_obvious_insight: In a standards vacuum, the first packaged evidence format an audit firm accepts becomes the de facto standard, as SOC 2 report formats did for cloud. Auditors are also under pressure to have an answer.
first_30_days: Recruit 2 former Big-4 SOX auditors and write 25 agent controls. Run free readiness workshops for 10 controllers already piloting agents in AP or close, and convert 2-3 to paid assessments.

title: Ship-Anywhere Prices for Pickup-Only Auction Lots
one_liner: Embed binding, lot-level delivered prices and a booked load-out window into online auction listings, so pickup-only machinery, estate and surplus lots attract national bidders, with the broker taking a cut of freight and the auctioneer sharing the hammer-price uplift.
customer: Regional auctioneers and liquidators selling machine tools, farm and construction equipment, restaurant and commercial surplus, estates and government surplus on HiBid, Proxibid, AuctionZip or their own sites. The buyer pays the freight.
problem: Pickup-only lots limit bidders to roughly a 100-200 mile radius and depress hammer prices. Existing help is an estimate (Proxibid embeds a uShip-based estimator showing approximate costs from comparable moves) or the buyer scrambling after winning, with a 3-7 day storage or removal deadline running. For a broker, pricing a 2,400-lb lathe at a rural site with one forklift and a Thursday-only load-out is a five-minute call. For a buyer it is a week of failed quotes, so out-of-area buyers simply do not bid.
solution: A listing-time tool. The auctioneer enters the pickup address and lot photos, dimensions and weight (a vision model plus a checklist estimates weight and cube from photos). It returns a binding delivered price by buyer ZIP, locked at bid time, including liftgate or loading, crating and a delivery window. On a win, it dispatches to a vetted pool of hot-shot, box truck, flatbed, lowboy and LTL carriers, books a load-out slot with the auction site's forklift operator, and pays carriers quickly. The auctioneer sees an A/B report of bidders per lot with and without delivered pricing.
why_now: Auction sales have moved largely online, and 2026 platform practice is to spell out freight and special-handling requirements and add approval steps before bidders commit to shipping charges. Vision models can now estimate weight and dimensions from listing photos well enough to quote. Small-load carriers (hot-shot, box truck) are plentiful because the freight market is soft and small carriers need loads.
revenue_model: 15-25% gross margin on freight, since small specialty loads carry higher broker margins than truckload. Typical freight ticket is $400-$1,800. Optionally share 5% of freight with the auctioneer, and later charge a per-lot fee tied to verified hammer-price uplift.
non_obvious_insight: The auctioneer's real problem is not shipping, it is bidder radius. Buyers do not bid on what they cannot price, so quote friction, not freight cost, kills out-of-area bids, which makes pre-bid freight pricing a hammer-price lever that can pay for itself. Also, the binding constraint at rural sites is the single forklift and a narrow load-out window, which no marketplace models. Solve that and carriers love the load because dwell is short.
first_30_days: Sign 5 auctioneers with many pickup-only lots. Concierge-price 50 lots by hand (form plus broker phone calls) and add a 'delivered to your ZIP' link in the lot description. Compare unique bidders and hammer price against matched control lots. Ship 40 lots under existing brokerage authority, and collect the freight margin only. Test estate sales and government surplus as second segments.

title: Signed Live Recordings from Every Small Venue
one_liner: A cheap box that records a small venue's mixing-desk multitrack, signs it with time and place, and delivers the artist a 'recorded live tonight' release within hours.
customer: Touring indie artists (per-show packages) and small venues of 25-500 capacity (hosts and revenue partners), later promoters and ticketing.
problem: The one thing AI cannot fabricate is a specific night in a specific room. Yet tens of thousands of small shows happen nightly with no recording, while generative music floods the shelf. Bandcamp's AI ban made it a natural home for human-made music, and artists have few new products to sell there.
solution: Software on a mini-PC or a $300-500 box connects to common digital consoles (Behringer X32/Midas-class, Allen & Heath) over USB or network to capture multitrack audio. It timestamps with network time and location, signs a C2PA audio manifest, auto-mixes with ML, and delivers a release and shareable page within hours. Venues get a share of sales, and a public ledger builds over time.
why_now: C2PA supports audio, generative music has made 'real and live' a scarcity signal, cheap mini-PCs and ML auto-mixing exist, and Bandcamp is positioned as a human-only marketplace.
revenue_model: $99-199 per show for the artist, or $79/month per venue plus 20% of release sales, with hardware leased at about $399.
non_obvious_insight: Provenance of place and time is unforgeable in a way that process proof is not. A live album also turns authenticity into a revenue-producing product instead of a cost.
first_30_days: Wire up 5 friendly venues in one city with X32 consoles. Hand-mix the first shows. Sell 'live release in 24 hours' to 20 touring bands at $99 through booking agents, and track Bandcamp sales.

title: Independent Collateral Audits for GPU-Backed Loans
one_liner: A floorplan-audit business for private credit: physically verify, monitor and value the GPUs that secure a fast-growing pile of debt.
customer: Mid-market private credit funds, family-office lenders, equipment-finance arms and ABS trustees with GPU-backed facilities. Neocloud borrowers are a second payer, since verified collateral lowers their cost of capital.
problem: Over $20 billion of GPU-backed debt existed by early 2026, typically advancing 50-70% of appraised value, yet the resale value depends on obsolescence assumptions that are unsettled. Two large neoclouds use depreciation schedules of six and four years on similar hardware. Lenders mostly rely on borrower-provided reports and cannot see the rack, so they cannot confirm that serial numbers exist, are powered, are utilized and are located where the collateral schedule says.
solution: Borrow the car-dealer floorplan audit playbook. Field technicians verify serial numbers via BMC/IPMI readouts and photos, check rack location and power draw, sample cluster utilization through read-only telemetry attestations, review hosting contracts, insurance and cooling health, and grade condition. Deliver a quarterly report to the lender, then build continuous monitoring and a published GPU residual-value index.
why_now: GPU-backed credit scaled from experiment to institutional product in 2025-26. The next-generation architecture transition in 2026 and the rolling-off of 2023-24 contracts make collateral quality the central credit question, and lenders new to the asset class have no in-house inspectors.
revenue_model: $5-25k per site audit and $2-8k per month for monitoring, paid by lenders and sometimes borrowers. Later, data license revenue from the residual-value index.
non_obvious_insight: A GPU loan looks like equipment finance but behaves like tech inventory concentrated in a few sites. The missing service is not analytics but a trusted human in the room. Aircraft and auto-floorplan lenders solved this decades ago, and a small team of ex-data-center technicians plus one equipment-finance lawyer can do the same.
first_30_days: Team up two ex-data-center technicians with an equipment-finance lawyer. Approach 10 mid-market lenders and GPU-lease brokers. Offer one first audit at cost for a lender-borrower pair. Standardize the deliverable (serial check, photos, power and uptime, contract review) and publish an anonymized sample report to win the next five audits.

title: Scan-Before-Buyout: Digital Memory and Game Assets
one_liner: Capture homes and streets in flood buyouts and burn zones in game-engine-grade 3D before demolition. The program pays for compliance and memorial; asset licensing to games and film is upside.
customer: County and state hazard-mitigation offices running buyouts, their historic-preservation consultants, and community foundations or long-term recovery groups funding memorials. Secondary buyers are game studios, VFX houses and XR training vendors.
problem: Buyouts demolish hundreds of 50-year-old homes. Federal funding triggers historic-property review, and the mitigation is often recorded documentation costing thousands per structure and producing a binder nobody opens. Families lose the physical record of their home and street, and the neighborhood dissolves undocumented. Only about 13% of affected Palisades owners have started rebuilding, so many lots sit for years. Game and film studios pay for authentic real-world environments that are hard to source.
solution: A crew of ex-game and VFX 3D artists uses Gaussian-splat or photogrammetry capture to scan exteriors, streetscapes and, with owner consent, interiors in an afternoon per home. Deliverables: (a) a compliance-grade documentation package, (b) a walkable keepsake file for each family, and (c) a de-identified 'American small-town' building kit licensed to studios, with revenue share to the community memorial fund.
why_now: Post-2024/25 flood buyouts are reaching demolition, and BRIC's $1B was reinstated in March 2026. Capture cost collapsed with splatting tools and phone-grade scanning. Game and VFX layoffs put skilled 3D artists on the market (Ubisoft headcount fell from 18,666 to 16,590 and EA's new owners plan AI-driven cost cuts), while studios need cheaper environment art.
revenue_model: Government or foundation contracts of $1,500-4,000 per structure or $40-150K per neighborhood, an optional $49 family keepsake often paid by a recovery fund, and five-figure per-studio licenses for the asset kit with revenue share to the county.
non_obvious_insight: The compliance mandate pays the bills, not the games market. Creative-industry tooling makes a documentation chore that nobody enjoys far cheaper, and turns it into a bereavement product and a licensable asset library. The county gets a better deliverable and a revenue share instead of a cost center.
first_30_days: Offer a free pilot street of 10 homes to a buyout manager in a post-flood region (western North Carolina or the Texas Hill Country). Collect owner releases. Deliver the splats plus a template mitigation stipulation a state preservation office can accept. Sell an anonymized kit on Fab, Sketchfab or the Unity store to test demand. Pitch consulting firms for subcontract work and a community foundation for the memorial grant.

title: Rent-a-Robot Creature Actors for Haunts and Events
one_liner: A rental troupe of costumed quadruped and humanoid robots, with operators and safety systems, for haunted attractions, festivals, conventions and immersive shows.
customer: Haunted attractions, seasonal theme-park events, festivals and conventions, immersive theatre producers and brand activations.
problem: Haunts struggle to hire and retain actors, and scares repeat. Fans love character robots (Disney's droids), but building one is expensive and risky, so small producers cannot offer them.
solution: Buy off-the-shelf sub-$5k quadrupeds and $6-16k humanoids and fit them with fabricated creature shells. Add a director's tablet for scripted and remote-driven behaviors, geofencing and e-stops, and insurance. Rent at $800-2,500 per night with an operator.
why_now: Cheap quadrupeds and humanoids with open-source locomotion are available, entertainment robots are already common in China, and Halloween is five weeks away.
revenue_model: Nightly rental plus operator fee, then creature shell and kit sales and character licensing.
non_obvious_insight: The hard part is not the robot, it is the show: safety envelope, character design, logistics and insurance. Amortizing hardware over 100+ nights a year makes this a creature-troupe service business, not a robotics company.
first_30_days: Lease 2 robots for about $6k and build two creature shells. Book 3-5 haunts and one convention for October and November at about $1,000 per night. Get event insurance and a written safety protocol.

title: Rainbows End Book Scanning With Chain of Custody
one_liner: Vernor Vinge's destructive mass digitization of a library, run as a service where the AI customer is owner of record and gets clean text plus a custody certificate, never resold scans.
customer: Specialist and mid-tier model builders (legal, medical, engineering and regional-language models) and enterprises training internal models. The buyer is the head of data or general counsel.
problem: After the Bartz v. Anthropic ruling (fair use for buying and scanning print books) and the $1.5 billion settlement over pirated copies, buy-and-scan is the defensible path. But it takes procurement across thousands of sellers, cutters, production scanners, QA and custody records. Only frontier labs have that muscle (the Project Panama disclosures in 2026 showed how large it was).
solution: Acquire books on the customer's behalf under a bill of sale so the customer is owner of record. Scan under work-for-hire, deliver OCR text and a chain-of-custody ledger (ISBN, invoice, copy serial number, cut and pulp certificate), and retain no digital copies. Focus on niches frontier labs skip: out-of-print trade and technical manuals, legal treatises, closing corporate and law-firm libraries, university deaccessions and regional-language books. A rare-edition triage rule sends scarce books to libraries or an archive instead of the cutter.
why_now: The Project Panama disclosures, the 2025 settlement and public backlash over 'book burning' have made provenance a line item for legal teams. Specialist labs want clean data but lack ops. Production scanners and hydraulic cutters are cheap and off the shelf.
revenue_model: Per-book fee (about $1.50-3), acquisition cost pass-through plus 10-20% procurement margin, typically $25-100k per project, plus a premium for custody-certificate audits.
non_obvious_insight: The Bartz reasoning covers a lab scanning books it owns for its own training, not reselling the scans. The whole business must therefore be structured as an agent working for the owner, not as a data vendor. The scarce input is not scanning but acquiring legally owned physical copies of niche material at scale, and the certificate is what counsel actually buys.
first_30_days: Spend about $25k on a hydraulic cutter and two production scanners. Buy about 10,000 books from library Friends sales and estate lots in one domain (for example legal treatises). Run a 5,000-book pilot for a legal-AI or medical-AI startup, using a custody-certificate template reviewed by copyright counsel.
